newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU nears deal to strengthen voice on world stage.
newsitem.headline: EU nears deal to strengthen voice on world stage.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers, seeking to give the 15-nation bloc a stronger voice in world diplomacy, are inching closer to agreement on a new foreign policy structure.
Although a number of tricky details remain to be solved before a summit in Amsterdam next month, officials said on Tuesday the essential outline of an agreement had begun to take shape.
"We should come out of Amsterdam with the tools needed," French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier.
Many in the EU have been critical of its apparent inability to take decisions quickly and effectively when foreign policy crises erupt.
"Nobody wants to go on as we have been," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said after hosting a negotiating session on a new EU treaty.
The EU has already unofficially agreed to create a forward planning unit whose main task will be to coordinate the bloc's response to foreign policy crises such as Bosnia and Zaire.
Under one plan being considered, a secretary general for the European Union would be appointed to run the new body and represent the EU abroad as its "voice".
A number of countries have shied away from past plans to create such a post, fearing to give one person too high a profile. But some form of coordinating position is likely to be agreed.
EU policy, meanwhile, would be set in two phases.
First, heads of state and government would agree a set of foreign policy goals -- indentifying areas where the Union had an interest and stating what those interests are.
The decisions on these goals would be taken unanimously, in effect giving a veto to each EU country.
Once a position was agreed, the decision on what to do in a given situation would be taken by foreign ministers based on plans drawn up by the forward planning unit.
A number of countries, notably France and Germany, have been pushing for the second decision to be taken by majority vote.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said his country, once vehementy opposed to any talk of majority voting, would be willing to consider this, but he indicated he has "reservations" about the idea.
London would insist, he said, on a country retaining the right to veto a policy decision which ran against its national interest.
But he also endorsed an idea -- first raised to meet the concerns of the bloc's neutrals -- of so-called "constructive abstenion".
Under this concept, a country not willing to agree a foreign policy action but not having any reason to block others from conducting it, would simply let them go ahead.
